questions.q: What was proto-industrialisation, and how did the factory system emerge?

answer.text: Even before factories appeared, there was large-scale industrial production for an international market. This is called proto-industrialisation. Merchants in the towns supplied money and raw material to peasants and artisans in the countryside, who spun and wove cloth in their own homes. This linked town merchants with village producers, though production was not yet based in factories.

The earliest factories in England came up around the 1730s, and the cotton industry expanded rapidly. Inventions such as the spinning jenny and, above all, James Watt's steam engine allowed machines to be powered and workers to be brought together under one roof, with supervision and discipline. Yet hand labour did not disappear at once, and industrialisation spread slowly and unevenly.

questions.q: How did British rule affect industrialisation in India?

answer.text: Before British rule, India was the world's leading exporter of cotton textiles, and ports such as Surat and Masulipatnam thrived on this trade.

Under British rule, machine-made cloth from Manchester flooded India, and Indian weavers lost their markets and income, so that India's rich handicraft industries declined — a process of deindustrialisation.

Indian factories rose only from the mid-nineteenth century, with the first cotton mill set up in Bombay in 1854 and jute mills in Bengal. Indian entrepreneurs like the Tatas invested, though they faced stiff competition and controls from the British.

answer: Thus colonial policy first ruined traditional industry and only later allowed a limited modern industry to grow.
